text: The query result has a TotalSalesAmount column and an OrderCount column already -- you could drag either straight onto a card. This report uses DAX measures instead, because measures keep recalculating correctly once filters get involved, and a raw column dragged on only works today by coincidence.

First measure: Total Sales, equal to SUM of CategoryPerformanceSnapshot TotalSalesAmount. SUM adds up every value currently visible to the measure -- every category if nothing's filtering, or just one category once a slicer narrows it down in the next lesson.

Second measure: Order Count, equal to SUM of CategoryPerformanceSnapshot OrderCount. Notice it's SUM, not DISTINCTCOUNT. The actual counting of distinct orders already happened back in the T-SQL query -- OrderCount is a column of pre-counted numbers, one per category. Summing those numbers gives the right total. DISTINCTCOUNT here would count how many different OrderCount values exist, which is a meaningless number.

Third measure builds on the first two: Average Order Value, equal to DIVIDE of Total Sales and Order Count. DIVIDE is used instead of a plain slash because it returns blank instead of an error if Order Count is ever zero for a filtered category -- a real possibility once the slicer in the next lesson is live.

All three live in the Power BI model as measures, not baked into the T-SQL and not as calculated columns -- which means every card, chart, and table that uses them stays correct automatically, with nothing duplicated.
With the three measures built, next lesson adds a category slicer and formats everything for a reader who's glancing at this during a meeting, not studying it.
